source_title: Moving up from the midwest — landlords are leeches
post_title: Moving up from the midwest — landlords are leeches
post_body:
Moving up from the midwest, The landlords in State College are leeches

I feel like its needed that I say, I have lived in the south and Midwest my whole life. The northeast is uncharted territory for me.
We are being charged three months rent to move in, a pet privilege fee, and pet deposit. All totaling around $3K to move into an apartment that is lesser quality and space than any other Ive lived in.
Note that it's illegal for them to require 2 mos security deposit after the first year. So if you renew this lease, they owe you 1 month's worth back after the first year is up.
Also, requiring pet deposit plus 2 mos security is almost certainly illegal under Pennsylvania rental law. Who's the company?
I threatened to sue The Apartment Store over some fishy business with security deposits and ended up doubling my money; happy to help you dig through the rules if you want to pursue it, though google knows as much as I do. Of course there is something to be said for not antagonizing your landlord while you still live there.
Welcome to State College.
"Last month's rent" and "Pet deposit" are both just part of the security deposit for the purposes of PA rental law, so they're still over the two month legal limit. They cannot hold more money than that no matter what names they put on it. (But I am not a lawyer; talk to one if you really want to get into it.)
Pet deposits are their own separate thing that doesn't apply to the security deposit. They can't use it as a security deposit, that would be against PA rental law. Idk if there is a mechanism to get it back at the end of a lease. I'm not a lawyer so you'll have to look into that.
My understanding is that the pet fee is fine. But if it is a deposit you are supposed to get back, it counts as part of the security deposit.              From some lawyers:
Is my landlord permitted to hold a "pet deposit" in addition to my regular security deposit?
The Landlord and Tenant Act in Pennsylvania does not allow for a separate pet deposit. A pet deposit is viewed in the same manner as any security deposit and the landlord is subject to the same limitations which are described above, that is, no more than two months' security deposit may be held for the first year of the lease and, after the first year of the lease no more than one month's security deposit may be held. This includes a pet deposit.
I think most landlords operating out of college towns take advantage of tenants because they (sometimes rightfully) think college students aren't smart enough to realize it. ARPM and other related property managers are absolutely horrendous!
Since it's most students first time living in an apartment they are often unaware of what to expect and of what questions they should be asking when they move in. As a result they get stuck in bad situations and get screwed over.
There's three reasons why the landlords get away with it:
Students (and people in general) often don't know their rights.
It's a pain to try and fight them because they know the game.
It's expensive to fight and students often don't have the money.
Our place burned down before we moved in. I never moved in. A year later, Continental Real Estate Management askes me to pay them over $10,000. I say, no. They press, I point out PA law says if the place is uninhabitable, you can't charge rent (the place was only rebuilt after my lease run out). They backed down.
Landlord tried keeping my security deposit for no reason. Spent about 30 minutes talking to a free attorney with PSU.
Landlord Venmoed me all of the money within an hour of the attorney sending him an email saying that we would take this to court otherwise. Highly recommend
Honestly living in a college town is mentally (and financially) draining. Especially when you come from a big city.
It's a very beautiful town but it's also definitely not for everyone. And it's not even about the services in State College (which aren't bad), just the feeling of being a town in the middle of nowhere that is the size of a compound is weird.
But oh well, it's only temporary anyways.
Rents are generally higher in the Northeast than in the South and Midewest (I live in Texas now).
That said, yes - you are correct.
I'm fortunately in this boad. My landlord has offered reduction in rent for my work clearing the driveway in winter and lawncare in the warmer months. Also chipped in some cash for me to do minor maintenance like powerwashing the siding and touchup paint inside. Could not ask for a better setup.
it's bad in literally every college town... landlords and more well-off people who buy up real estate have the advantage of charging more money for cheaper apartments because college students need to be able to walk to campus -- hey if people will continue to pay 1000/month for a shared room in a cheap apartment with no utilities and no laundry then that price will never go down
The broker fee is the worst part. The broker literally posts a lazy Craigslist ad, gets a million applicants immediately, passes them to the landlord, and gets a month's rent for what I can't imagine ever takes more than an hour or two of work.
That said the actual landlords I have had in State College were way worse than anything in Boston (ok, ok, Somerville).
This is common for student housing at every major university. Students are transient and inexperienced, so landlords tend to take advantage of them.
If you aren't an undergrad, I don't suggest living near campus. Only some parts of State College allow undergrad rentals, which causes rents to be artificially inflated for shit properties because there is nothing these kids can do about it. Find a place a couple miles away like Park Forest, down at the south end of Blue Course, or over in Boalsburg.
This is in most college towns and honestly, PSU is not the most expensive lol. It is high, dont get me wrong. Thats why I moved farther out! I suggest trying to find a private landlord instead of a larger property management company. Also, off campus should be the real answer! You can save way more than youll spend on commute.
They take advantage of college kids. They assume most of them either don't know they're getting screwed over or that they are too lazy to do something about it and they're usually right. You have to take steps to protect yourself. Document every interaction you have with them, usually by email, and save all your receipts for everything. It will come in handy at the end of the year
